paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Thermal radiation is electromagnetic radiation given off because of the heat-driven motion of particles in matter. Everything warmer than absolute zero gives it off. Along with conduction and convection, it is one of the basic ways heat moves from place to place.

paragraphs.heading: How it is made
paragraphs.text: Thermal energy is the kinetic energy of atoms and molecules moving at random. Those atoms and molecules are built from charged particles, protons and electrons. As the particles jostle, charges accelerate and dipoles oscillate. That produces linked electric and magnetic fields, which send out photons that carry energy away from the body. Like visible light, this radiation can keep travelling through a vacuum without end.

paragraphs.heading: From infrared to glowing
paragraphs.text: At room temperature most thermal radiation is infrared. Above about 525 °C (977 °F), enough of it is visible that the object glows, a glow called incandescence. The radiation is never a single frequency but a continuous spread, and temperature sets how that spread is shaped. At any temperature there is one frequency where the output peaks, and Wien's displacement law says this peak frequency is proportional to the absolute temperature.

paragraphs.heading: The perfect emitter
paragraphs.text: A black body is an ideal object in thermodynamic equilibrium whose surface absorbs every wavelength perfectly. It is also a perfect emitter, and its radiation is called black-body radiation. Real objects are compared with it through emissivity, their emission as a fraction of a black body's, so a black body scores one. At any one wavelength in equilibrium, a good absorber is also a good emitter, and a poor absorber a poor emitter. Planck's law gives the spread of a black body's radiation across frequencies.

paragraphs.heading: Sun, Earth and air
paragraphs.text: The Sun heats the Earth mainly by thermal radiation. Its photosphere is about 6000 K and gives off mostly visible light. Much of that light passes through the atmosphere to the ground, where it is absorbed or reflected. The ground then radiates like a black body at 300 K, at lower frequencies where the air is largely opaque. About 10% of this escapes to space, but most is absorbed and given off again by gases in the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Seeing heat
paragraphs.text: Thermal radiation can reveal things the eye cannot see. Thermographic cameras make pictures by sensing infrared, which can show how temperature varies across a scene and pick out objects warmer than their surroundings. In the dark they can find animals or people by their body heat. The cosmic microwave background is thermal radiation too.
